summary.text: In physics, motion is the change in position of an object over a given time, measured with respect to a reference frame.
Everything in the universe can be considered to be in motion, and spacetime, the fabric of the universe, is expanding.

facts.label: Milky Way speed
facts.value: About 600 km/s relative to nearby galaxies

facts.label: Hubble's law
facts.value: Distant galaxies are all moving away from Earth

facts.label: Kinematics scope
facts.value: Describes motion without considering its underlying causes

items.prompt: A sports scientist records a runner's stride length and speed over time without measuring the muscular forces pushing off the track. Which branch of physics covers this study?

options.label: Kinematics
Dynamics
Quantum mechanics
General relativity

items.explain: Kinematics describes how objects move—such as tracking distance, speed, or position—without examining the forces that cause the movement.

items.prompt: You are sitting completely still inside a high-speed train reading a book. Why does an observer standing on the train platform see you moving rapidly?

options.label: Your body experiences an active push while inside the carriage.
An object's motion is measured relative to an observer's frame of reference.
Classical physics states that all physical movement must be absolute.
Subatomic particles in your body are constantly expanding outward.

items.explain: Motion is relative to a reference frame, meaning you are at rest compared to the train around you, but moving relative to the stationary platform outside.

items.prompt: If a laboratory experiment pinpoints the exact position of a subatomic electron, what does quantum mechanics say about measuring its velocity at that exact moment?

options.label: Its velocity automatically drops to zero.
Its velocity can be calculated with complete precision at the same time.
Its velocity cannot be simultaneously determined with exact precision.
Its velocity transforms into a simple classical vector quantity.

items.explain: According to the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, the position and velocity of a subatomic particle cannot be measured simultaneously with complete accuracy.

items.prompt: A puck slides across smooth ice and continues moving in a straight line at a constant speed for a long distance. Why does it keep moving like this?

options.label: No net external force has acted on it to change its state of motion.
The puck creates an internal gravitational push that pulls it forward.
The overall expansion of spacetime pushes the puck across the ice surface.
Its subatomic particles are behaving exclusively like continuous waves.

items.explain: The law of inertia states that a body in motion will stay in motion at a constant speed and direction unless an outside force acts on it.

items.prompt: While standing in your room, you feel as though you are completely motionless. Why can you not easily feel the Earth orbiting the Sun at high speed?

options.label: Human senses are completely incapable of detecting any form of speed.
Earth's oceans absorb all physical movement, keeping land completely still.
Spacetime contracts around human bodies to cancel out planetary movement.
You move along with the Earth's mass and lack an obvious external reference frame.

items.explain: Large-scale movements are hard for humans to feel because we are connected to the moving mass of the planet and lack an obvious visual frame showing our motion.

items.prompt: Astronomers observe that distant galaxies across deep space are all moving away from Earth. What universal process accounts for this observation?

options.label: The Milky Way is spinning so fast that it repels all nearby galaxies.
Spacetime itself is expanding like a stretching rubber band.
Continental drift on Earth shifts our telescopes away from distant stars.
Strong gravitational forces at the center of Earth push space outward.

items.explain: Hubble's law verified that the fabric of spacetime is expanding, causing distant astronomical objects to move away from one another.

pack.title: Why Nothing Is Truly Still
pack.question: How does physics describe the movement of objects across different scales?

beats.title: Why Nothing Is Truly Still
beats.hook: Even when you sit completely still, you are traveling through space at hundreds of kilometers per second.

beats.prompt: Sort each physical scenario into the realm of mechanics used to describe its motion.

left.label: A planet moving in orbit around a star
An electron exhibiting both wave and particle behaviors
A projectile launched across a field
A subatomic particle whose exact position and speed cannot be known at the same time

beats.explain: Classical mechanics handles macroscopic objects moving much slower than light, such as planets and projectiles. Quantum mechanics describes subatomic phenomena like wave-particle duality and position uncertainty.

beats.prompt: One step in this explanation of physical motion is incorrect. Which step fails?

steps.text: Motion is defined as a change in an object's position over time relative to a reference frame.
Because there is no absolute reference frame, everything in the universe can be considered to be in motion.
Under classical rules, an object moving in deep space will naturally slow down and stop on its own without any outside force.
Therefore, an external force is required to alter an object's speed or direction.

beats.explain: The law of inertia states that a moving object remains in motion unless an external force acts upon it; it does not slow down by itself.

beats.prompt: You sit completely motionless in a chair inside your living room. What is your motion status according to physics?
beats.explain: An object can be stationary relative to its immediate surroundings while simultaneously moving relative to other reference frames, such as nearby galaxies or the cosmic background radiation.

choices.label: You are motionless relative to your room, but moving relative to frames like the cosmic microwave background.
You are in absolute rest because your house provides the one fixed baseline for the universe.
choices.feedback: Modern physics shows there is no absolute reference frame in the universe.

choices.label: You are completely stationary across all reference frames because your limbs are not walking.
choices.feedback: Motion depends on the chosen frame of reference; relative to distant galaxies, you move as Earth travels through space.

choices.label: You are traveling at the speed of light because all human bodies default to light speed on Earth.
choices.feedback: Classical mechanics describes macroscopic human bodies moving far slower than the speed of light.

beats.idea: Motion is a change in position over time relative to a reference frame, spanning from subatomic probabilities to expanding galactic space.

paragraphs.heading: What motion means
paragraphs.text: In physics, something is in motion when its position changes over time, measured against a reference frame. The idea covers fluids as well as solid objects. If an object's position does not change relative to that frame, it is said to be at rest, or stationary. Motion is written down with vector quantities: displacement pairs a distance with a direction, and velocity pairs a speed with a direction.

paragraphs.heading: Two ways to study it
paragraphs.text: Kinematics is the branch of physics that describes how things move without asking what makes them move. Dynamics is the branch that studies forces and how they change motion. Because modern physics holds that no absolute frame of reference exists, Newton's notion of absolute motion cannot be measured. Relative motion is an object's motion described from the frame that travels along with an observer, using relative position and relative velocity.

paragraphs.heading: Newton's three laws
paragraphs.text: First, a body at rest stays at rest and a moving body keeps moving unless an outside force acts on it; this is the law of inertia. Second, force equals the change in momentum per change in time, and for a constant mass F⃗ = ma⃗. Third, when one body pushes on a second, the second pushes back with a force of the same size in the opposite direction, so the first body is pushed backward. These laws were the first accurate mathematical model of bodies orbiting in space, and they put the motion of the heavens and of things on Earth under one explanation.

paragraphs.heading: Where the old rules stop
paragraphs.text: Classical mechanics handles large objects moving far slower than light, from projectiles and machine parts to spacecraft, planets, stars and galaxies, and it gives very accurate results there. Special relativity is the part of mechanics that compares every velocity with the speed of light c. General relativity brings in gravity, using differential geometry to describe a curved universe. At the level of atoms and smaller particles, quantum mechanics takes over, and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle means a subatomic particle's location and velocity cannot both be fixed at once.

paragraphs.heading: Motion you cannot feel
paragraphs.text: People are always moving, in many ways that are harder to notice than walking or waving an arm. Large-scale motions escape us for two reasons. Newton's laws, the third above all, stop us feeling the motion of a mass we are attached to, and there is no obvious frame of reference to show us that we are moving. At the smaller scales, on the other hand, these motions are too tiny for our senses to detect.

paragraphs.heading: Earth's ride through space
paragraphs.text: The Milky Way spins around its dense centre, so the Sun travels in a circle inside the galaxy, and the planets and their moons travel with it. Away from the central bulge, stars typically move at 210 to 240 kilometres per second. The galaxy as a whole is thought to move at about 600 kilometres per second relative to nearby galaxies, or about 582 kilometres per second measured against the cosmic microwave background. Spacetime itself is also expanding, a change in the nature of the universe rather than ordinary movement, and Edwin Hubble showed that distant galaxies are all moving away from Earth.
